title: The low-water clause nobody reads
subtitle: Rhine and Danube levels can rewrite an itinerary mid-week. It is in the contract.

text: Low water can mean coaches, or swapping to a sister ship.
sub: When a stretch becomes too shallow to transit, lines reroute: guests move by road to the next town, or two vessels trade guests so each keeps its own reach of river.

title: What a rerouted week looks like

items.head: A day by coach
items.body: You still see the town. You see it after a road transfer rather than from your own deck.

items.head: A ship swap
items.body: Two vessels trade guests mid-river so neither crosses the shallow stretch. Luggage moves with you.

items.head: A reordered itinerary
items.body: The same towns in a different order, sometimes a substitution. The captain's call, not the brochure's.

items.head: A night in a hotel ashore
items.body: Uncommon, but it happens. Ask who funds it before you book, not while you are packing.

points.label: A long dry spell
points.value: The classic low-water risk on the Rhine and Danube, and it can arrive in any month.

points.label: Snowmelt and storms
points.value: Levels can also run too high. Bridges and locks set a ceiling as well as a floor.

points.label: Shoulder weeks
points.value: Often the calmer water and the quieter towns at once. Usually where I point people.

points.label: The clause itself
points.value: Read it once. It tells you whether a rerouted week is compensated or simply absorbed.

left.label: At booking
items: Is a sister ship in reach?

right.label: At the pier
items: You learn it from a notice

text: Water level is weather. The clause is a choice.
sub: No line controls the river, and I hold none of them to that. But how a rerouted week is handled and funded is written down before you sail. Read it, or have someone read it.

title: Save this before you pay a river deposit
body: Or send me the sailing you're considering and I'll tell you how that line handles low water.
